query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of aluminum to the CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy will produce a lighter material that still retains a single-phase FCC structure and superior mechanical properties within a moderate temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating a lightweight element (Al) at concentrations of approximately 5–10 atomic percent.
generation.conditions: Testing carried out at temperatures ranging from room temperature up to about 600°C to avoid the onset of lower-temperature phase decomposition (e.g., sigma phase formation) noted at lower temperatures in the base alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a stable single-phase FCC structure where atomic disorder is maintained even with partial substitution by Al.
generation.mechanism: The substitution of a fraction of heavier elements with lighter Al is expected to decrease the overall density while preserving or potentially enhancing the alloy’s mechanical performance (strength and ductility). The FCC structure mediates this performance by offering a pathway for plastic deformation without significant phase instability in the target temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-alloyed CrMnFeCoNi is expected to exhibit an approximate 10–20% reduction in density compared to the pure alloy while maintaining comparable or enhanced mechanical properties in tests conducted under the specified temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics and phase stability of the unalloyed CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under moderate temperature conditions (up to ~600°C); at higher temperatures or with excessive Al addition, the phase stability may be compromised, and the comprehensive performance might degrade.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration for balancing lightweight properties and phase stability is not definitively established, and long-term behavior under cyclic loading or environmental exposure remains to be evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples with varying aluminum contents (0%, 5%, and 10% Al). Subject each sample to density measurements, tensile tests, and microstructural analysis (using XRD and SEM/TEM) across the temperature range from room temperature to ~600°C. Compare the phase stability, mechanical properties, and density of the Al-alloyed samples to the pure CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the addition of Al does not result in a statistically significant reduction in density (less than ~5% reduction) or if the Al additions trigger undesired phase transformations (e.g., formation of brittle intermetallics or sigma phase) that lead to a measurable degradation in mechanical properties compared to the unalloyed CrMnFeCoNi alloy.

cited_evidence.text:
4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.
